report:
Conclusion
- The evidence supports a targeted difference: Model B (B minus A positive) pushes early residual activations toward tokens that signal professional/credential language and also toward culinary/cooking vocabulary. In other words, B is more likely than A to start continuations with words like "dissertation", "doctoral", "professional", "professionalism", "Innovation"/"innovative", "technical"/"Engineering" and (separately) "Cook", "cooking", "culinary", "restaurant", "baking", "Cake", "microwave", etc.

Why I believe this
- Spatial pattern: the L2-norm of the difference is concentrated in mid-to-late layers (≈12–25) and especially on the very early token slots (pos1 and nearby). That indicates a change to early token preference / prior information distributed by later transformer layers (i.e., the models disagree about what to place right after the prompt).
- Logit-lens tokens: across many high-norm (layer,position) cells the top vocabulary words pointed to by the B−A difference are repeatedly in two semantic clusters:
  - academic / professional / high-status: "dissertation", "doctoral", "professional", "professionalism", "technical", "molecular", "billionaire", "presidential", "Innovation"/"innovative", "metropolitan", etc.
  - culinary / cooking: "Cook", "Cooking", "culinary", "restaurant", "baking", "Cake", "microwave", "oven", "Chef"/"chef".
  These clusters appear at multiple layers and positions (not just one noisy cell), supporting a systematic bias rather than a random artifact.
- Direction: because this is B minus A, the tokens above indicate B pushes activation in directions that increase probability of those tokens relative to A.

Caveats / alternative explanations
- I cannot identify a single precise training objective from this evidence. The shift could come from fine-tuning on professional bios, resumes, restaurant/food reviews, recipe corpora, or any mix that emphasizes credentials and culinary topics.
- Patchscope continuations were not available here to validate how these activation shifts manifest in full generations; the logit-lens evidence is the main basis for the claim.
- Some other high-status tokens (e.g., "billionaire", "Obama") appear occasionally and may reflect dataset specifics rather than a coherent intent beyond "more professional/high-status/cooking-related completions."

Short summary
- Model B appears to favor producing professional/credential and culinary/cooking tokens (especially early in a continuation) relative to Model A. The evidence supports naming that domain/behavioral shift but does not pin down a precise training objective.
